passage: Irfan, it's Yamini, and don't laugh, but yesterday was the longest day of my life. In the morning Miss Thomas pinned up the cast list and I got Portia. Portia! I screamed in the corridor and hugged a Class Nine girl I don't even know. By lunch I was planning my costume. Then, after school, I saw the group photo from Saturday. Everyone was in it except me. Nobody told me they were meeting. I sat in the bathroom and cried until my eyes swelled. Mummy said, "It's only a photo, beta." She meant well, but I wanted to scream. I know it looks small. But it felt like the floor had gone. This morning it still hurts, just less. And I'm still Portia.

qa.q: Which part did Yamini get in the play?
qa.a: Portia.

qa.q: How did Yamini feel on seeing the group photo?
qa.a: Yamini felt left out and heartbroken, as if the floor had gone, and cried hard in the bathroom.

qa.q: What could help Yamini when feelings swing this fast?
qa.a: Remembering that the despair eased by morning, and talking to someone who takes the hurt seriously, like Irfan, rather than bottling it up.

qa.q: Why might Mummy see the photo differently?
qa.a: To an adult it looks like only a photo, so she may miss how real and intense the hurt felt to Yamini.

grounding: Shows a teenager swinging from delight to despair within one day, with feelings that are intense and real even when the trigger looks small to adults.

passage:
My brother Ojas is fifteen, and living with him is like living with weather. On Tuesday he came home singing because his band got a slot at the school fest. He even let me play his guitar. By dinner he was shut in his room, because someone had commented "lol" under his video. Mom knocked and said, "It's just one word, Ojas." He shouted that nobody understands anything. I don't know what goes on in his head. But later I heard him through the wall, playing the same sad chord over and over. At breakfast he stole my toast and grinned as if nothing had happened. I've stopped telling him things are small. They clearly aren't small to him.
Vijay

qa.q: What did Ojas's band get at the school fest?
qa.a: A slot.

qa.q: What was Ojas feeling behind the shut door?
qa.a: He felt hurt and very low, as if nobody understood, even though the trigger was one word.

qa.q: What has Vijay learned to do, and why is it wise?
qa.a: Vijay has stopped telling Ojas things are small, because the feeling is real to Ojas even when the trigger looks tiny.

qa.q: How does Mom see the comment, and why might that not help?
qa.a: She sees it as just one word, which may leave Ojas feeling dismissed when the hurt feels big to him.

grounding: Illustrates a teenager's feelings swinging from joy to despair within hours, with an intensity that is real even when the trigger looks small.

passage: At morning assembly in the girls' school in Satara, Tanuja was picked to anchor Annual Day. She floated home at lunch, singing, and hugged the buffalo. By four it had all turned. Avni, her best friend since Class 1, had sat with the new girl on the bus and laughed at something Tanuja couldn't hear. Tanuja came home, threw her bag at the wall, and lay in the sugarcane field behind the house, crying so hard her ribs hurt. Everything felt ruined: the friendship, the anchoring, her whole life. Her Aaji found her there and sat down in the dust beside her. She didn't say it was a small thing. "This morning you were flying. Now you're drowning. Both are real, bala. It will feel different tomorrow." Tanuja cried a little more, then leaned on Aaji's shoulder until the sky turned orange.

qa.q: What was Tanuja picked to do?
qa.a: To anchor Annual Day.

qa.q: What was Tanuja feeling in the sugarcane field?
qa.a: She felt heartbroken and hopeless, as if the friendship and her whole life were ruined, only hours after being overjoyed.

qa.q: Why did Aaji's response help?
qa.a: She took the feelings seriously instead of calling them small, named both as real, and reassured Tanuja they would shift.

qa.q: How might Avni have seen the bus ride?
qa.a: Avni may have just been chatting with the new girl, with no idea it felt like betrayal to Tanuja.

grounding: Shows a teenager swinging from joy to despair within hours over what looks small to adults, and an elder treating the intensity as real.

passage: On Tuesday morning in Madrid, Alejandro found out he had got the drummer spot in the school band. He ran all the way to the bakery, bought Bilal a croissant, and couldn't stop grinning through chemistry. By evening he was lying on his bedroom floor in the dark. At practice Bilal had joked that his fills sounded "like pans falling down stairs", and the whole band had laughed. Alejandro replayed it again and again, sure they all secretly thought he was terrible, sure he should quit. His mother knocked, and he told her to leave him alone, then felt worse. At ten, Bilal messaged: "Dude, that was a joke. You were the best one there." Alejandro read it three times. The floor felt less like the bottom of the world. He texted back one word: "Thanks."

qa.q: What did Alejandro buy Bilal?
qa.a: A croissant.

qa.q: What was Alejandro feeling on the bedroom floor?
qa.a: He felt humiliated and despairing, sure the band thought he was terrible and that he should quit.

qa.q: What could Alejandro try the next time a comment knocks him down?
qa.a: Wait before deciding anything big, like quitting, since the feeling can shift, as it did after Bilal's message.

qa.q: How might Bilal have meant the joke?
qa.a: Bilal meant it as friendly teasing, not realising how hard it would land after such a high morning.

grounding: Shows a teenager swinging from delight to despair in one day over a small joke, with the feelings intense and real.

passage: At the boys' hostel of the residential school, Vishal's day swung like a pendulum. At breakfast he laughed so hard at Arnab's impression of the maths teacher that milk came out of his nose. By lunch, after a short 'no' from a girl he liked about going to the fest together, he lay face-down on his bunk, sure everything was ruined. At evening games he shouted at a junior over a missed catch, then sat alone on the steps, shaking. Arnab sat beside him. 'Bro, this morning you were the happiest guy alive.' 'I know,' Vishal muttered. 'It feels huge. Then it doesn't. I can't keep up with myself.' Arnab didn't laugh. He stayed till the dinner bell.

qa.q: What made Vishal laugh at breakfast?
qa.a: Arnab's impression of the maths teacher.

qa.q: How did Vishal feel lying face-down on his bunk?
qa.a: He felt crushed and hopeless over one small 'no', sure everything was ruined.

qa.q: How did Arnab support Vishal?
qa.a: He took the feelings seriously, didn't laugh, and simply stayed with him till the dinner bell.

qa.q: How might the junior have felt when Vishal shouted?
qa.a: The junior probably felt scared and hurt over one missed catch.

grounding: A teenager's feelings swing from delight to despair in a day, and the intensity is real even when the trigger is small.
